claims.statement: The prod host backup is the operator's host-level disaster recovery: a restic snapshot of every stateful prod service (Forgejo, Komodo, Keycloak, agent-db and both Mongo instances), the service config directories, and the release APKs a rebuild cannot reproduce, pushed to a remote the operator controls. It is explicitly not the same system as feature 073's per-user collection backups, and neither replaces the other: a user's own backup does not protect the host, and the host snapshot cannot be restored per user.

The backup is config-as-code: the scripts, systemd units and a checksum manifest live in infrastructure-as-code/backup/, and the host runs copies installed at ~/backup/*.sh and ~/.config/systemd/user/homelab-backup*; that directory's README is the canonical install/update/verify contract.

Every dump runs through a single run_dump path that never fails the script: a failed dump leaves a DUMP-FAILED-<name> marker inside the snapshot, the remaining dumps and the restic upload and retention still run, and the run's exit status reports the failure so the unit's OnFailure= alert fires. This isolation exists because the original script's Forgejo step was the only step without a fallback, so under set -e its failure skipped every database dump and the off-site upload.

Each dump is validated after it is written, in its own format and against a per-dump minimum size, and a dump that fails either check is treated exactly like a failed dump command. The formats are per dump: a plain Postgres dump must end at the pg_dump/pg_dumpall completion marker, the forge's custom-format database dump must start with the PGDMP magic, a Mongo archive must pass gzip -t, and the forge data tar must list git/repositories/, gitea/conf/app.ini and gitea/jwt/ — the signing keys without which every issued token and the Actions OIDC identity change on restore. The minimum may legitimately be near zero — agent-db's is 1 byte because agent_db has no tables by design, the gateway checkpointing in memory — so a non-empty test alone would be wrong.

A dump whose size falls below 50% of the same dump in the last good run raises a shrink alert naming the dump and both sizes, but the snapshot is still uploaded and the run still succeeds. An expected shrink is accepted once with backup.sh --ack-shrink <dump>, which writes a state file the next run consumes and deletes; the threshold is never raised instead, and only a fully good run rewrites the last-good manifest that the comparison is based on.

Dump staging must be on disk: /tmp on the prod host is a 29 G tmpfs, the Forgejo dump outgrew it, and the original script staged there, so backups failed every night from 2026-07-27 to 2026-10-22 and the outage was found by chance. backup.sh therefore stages under ~/backup/ and refuses a tmpfs staging filesystem before dumping anything, and backup.sh --check-staging reports the filesystem without backing anything up.

restic retention must group by tag, not by path: the call carries --tag homelab --group-by host,tags because the staging directory's name is random, so restic's default host,paths grouping put every snapshot in a group of one and pruned nothing. The same randomness is why the staleness check lists all homelab snapshots rather than using --latest, which is per path group.

Alerting has two independent paths onto one backlog item, titled 'Prod backup: failed or stale'. Path one is the run's own failure: backup.sh exits 1 and OnFailure=homelab-backup-alert@%n.service on homelab-backup.service runs backup-alert.sh failed <unit>, with a run killed by TimeoutStartSec=2h reported as hung rather than failed. The measured run time makes that timeout unambiguous: about 65 s for the eight-dump format (2026-10-29) against 8-10 min for the old single forgejo dump (2026-10-22..26). Path two is a separate 6-hourly staleness timer and service running backup-staleness.sh, which reads the newest homelab snapshot from the backup repository itself and alerts stale past 36 h, or staleness-unreadable when it cannot read the age at all - 'could not tell' is never reported as fresh. Neither the alert unit nor the staleness service declares OnFailure=, so a failing alert does not recurse and a stale check is not double-reported.

The second alerting path exists precisely because a run that never happens, a hung run, or an upload that silently did nothing fires no OnFailure; a heartbeat written by the run being checked would not be independent, and a CI-hosted check would need the restic password that decrypts every backup in Actions secrets. MCM_BACKUP_STALE_HOURS exists for tests only and no unit sets it.

backup-alert.sh puts every backup event on exactly one backlog item: it searches open issues for the exact title 'Prod backup: failed or stale' (no label filter, since an unknown label name is silently ignored), comments when the item exists and creates it labelled type/bug and priority/p1 by label id when it does not, never closes it, and a fully good run posts a recovered comment that no-ops when nothing is open.

The alert needs an issues-scoped token in a mode-600 file and the forge's local URL (MCM_FORGE_URL) in an env file beside it; the token is passed to curl through a header file rather than argv so ps and the journal never see it. A missing or loose token or an unset URL exits 3 and an HTTP failure exits 4, each printing 'alert NOT delivered' to the journal rather than failing silently, and the posted detail is redacted — URI user-info masked and any line naming a credential dropped.

INSTALLED.sha256 is the artefact that lets an operator with no repository checkout prove the host runs what the repository says: it lists every installable file as <sha256>  <path relative to $HOME> at the path the README's install block puts it, sorted so a regenerated list diffs cleanly. It is regenerated by scripts/backup-install-manifest.mjs --write and verified with --check, and a guard fails when the committed list disagrees with the directory or omits a new installable file — a stale list is worse than none, because the operator's sha256sum -c would then pass against an old script.

backup.sh holds no secret: the restic password comes from RESTIC_PASSWORD_FILE outside the script, the forge package token is read from a mode-600 file on disk, and every other credential (the Komodo Postgres user and password, the Mongo URIs) is read live from a compose env file or a running container, so no credential is ever assigned a literal in the committed script. The guard is both behavioural and textual: the script is scanned by the shared secret scanner and asserted to contain no credential-named variable assigned anything but an expansion.

The dump list is the part that must grow with the host: the original script dumped only Forgejo, Komodo and the object-store/nx-cache config directories and no application database, so a reboot that corrupted Forgejo's Postgres left Forgejo the only stateful service with a real backup. The standing rule is that adding a stateful service means adding its dump to backup.sh, with a minimum size and a format check.

The accepted gap in the alerting is that if the whole host, or the prod user's systemd manager, is down, both timers stop and the staleness check goes down with the backup. That is accepted rather than engineered around because the same state stops the forge, the application and every CI run, so it is loud rather than silent; what the two paths cover is the case that went unseen for three months, where the host is up and the backup is broken.

The backup scripts are guarded behaviourally rather than by inspection, and the guards run in guardrails.yml's naming job, whose node --test scripts/__tests__/*.test.mjs step picks them up automatically. The suites share one fake prod host, scripts/__tests__/host-shims.mjs — deliberately not named *.test.mjs so the glob does not collect it — which shims docker, restic, curl, systemctl and df first on PATH, records each call's argv, answers from a fixture, captures an absolute directory argument with its file sizes, dump-manifest.tsv and any *.tar listing (because backup.sh deletes its staging dir on exit), and never records an -H @file argument, which is how a token reaches curl; unshimmed tools (bash, python3, tar, gzip, stat) are real, so format checks run against real files. The harness is itself guarded twice: host-shims.test.mjs pins that a shim propagates stdout, stderr and exit codes and that a token's header file is never recorded, and host-shims-cleanup.test.mjs pins that each suite removes its temp root. backup-script.test.mjs runs backup.sh against that host and pins the measured failure modes, including that a failing forge dump still runs every other dump and still calls restic backup, the per-dump format and minimum verdicts, the eight forge-data excludes, shrink and ack-shrink, staging under ~/backup with tmpfs refused, --group-by host,tags on forget, and the absence of a literal credential; backup-units.test.mjs pins the unit wiring; backup-alert.test.mjs pins the exact forge API calls and the token never appearing in argv; backup-staleness.test.mjs pins 'unreadable is never fresh'; backup-install-manifest.test.mjs pins the committed manifest against the directory; and komodo-cron-retention.test.mjs pins the purge job as hourly, idempotent and touching only its own table.

The dump list is now eight dumps — forge-db, forge-data, komodo, keycloak, agent-db, mc-service-mongo, bff-mongo and release-apks. The single forge dump was split into a pg_dump custom-format database dump plus a tar of the forge's /data, and release-apks was added as the one registry artefact a rebuild cannot reproduce.

The forge data tar is deliberately uncompressed: restic chunks content-defined and de-duplicates an unchanged file, so a mostly-unchanged tar costs roughly the day's real change, whereas the old forgejo dump --type tar.gz changed from its first changed byte onwards and de-duplicated nothing — 19.8-21.1 GiB added to the repository every night.

The forge-data format check is a content check rather than only a listing check: the tar must list git/repositories/, gitea/conf/app.ini and gitea/jwt/, because a restore without the JWT signing keys changes every issued token and the Actions OIDC identity. The eight --exclude paths are pinned by backup-script.test.mjs, so adding or removing one is a deliberate decision about what a restore loses.

The komodo dump carries a maximum of 500 MB: exceeding it is not a failure but a warn-max verdict, which raises a komodo-oversize alert naming the dump and both sizes, still uploads the snapshot, and suppresses the recovered note so it cannot close the item the oversize alert just opened. The dump also excludes cron.job_run_details' rows (roles come from pg_dumpall --globals-only, each database psql lists from pg_dump --exclude-table-data). Separately, komodo-cron-retention.sql stops the table itself growing by installing the hourly pg_cron job purge-cron-run-history at 17 * * * *, which deletes runs older than 3 days; the file is applied by hand, safe to re-apply because it unschedules the job by jobid before creating it, and touches no other table.

release-apks is dumped from the forge's generic-package API using ~/backup/forge-package-token (mode 600, package read only) and MCM_FORGE_URL, as an uncompressed tar of release-apks/<version>/<file> covering every version and every file, paginated in pages of 50 because q= is a substring match that an unpaginated read silently truncates. A missing or loose token, or a version whose file list cannot be read, fails that dump alone: every other dump and the retention prune still run.

The install/verify contract rests on three host tokens, each created in the forge UI for this host alone with exactly one scope: ~/backup/forge-issue-token (issue read and write) for backup-alert.sh, ~/backup/forge-package-token (package read) for the release-apks dump, and ~/.config/mcm-forge-read-token (repository read) for the ~/mcm-main checkout, which clones through a credential helper so the token never enters the URL, argv or .git/config. MCM_FORGE_URL in ~/backup/alert.env names the forge as the host reaches it for both the alert and the APK dump, and the real host is never committed.

backup-alert.sh's reason vocabulary is closed — failed, hung, stale, staleness-unreadable, shrink, komodo-oversize, recovered — and an unknown reason exits 2 before any network call. The exit contract is 0 for delivered or nothing to do, 2 usage, 3 not configured (missing or non-600 token file, unset MCM_FORGE_URL) and 4 for a failed forge API call; exits 3 and 4 print 'alert NOT delivered' to the journal instead of failing silently, and only the failed reason consults the unit state, reporting a unit whose Result= is timeout as hung.

The once-after-install proof that the alerting works is an induced failure: point the run at a repository that does not exist with systemctl --user set-environment RESTIC_REPOSITORY=..., start homelab-backup.service, expect exit 1 and an 'alert delivered' line on the alert unit, and restore the default on the same line — an interrupted override stays set and every nightly fails until it is cleared with systemctl --user unset-environment RESTIC_REPOSITORY. The staleness path is exercised the same way with MCM_BACKUP_STALE_HOURS=0, which must produce an exit 1 and a stale comment on the same item.

A restore drill (spec 084 FR-006) is the only proof that a backup's contents can actually be restored, so it must be run after any change to what the backup carries and at least quarterly - a change to the dump format invalidates the previous proof. It must not be run between 03:00 and 04:00, because restic forget --prune needs an exclusive lock, so a drill still reading the repository at 03:30 fails that night's run loudly through the alert. It costs about 2 GB free under ~/backup and about 1.5 GB downloaded from the NAS, runs in a prod session, and never touches a live service: the scratch containers start with --network none and need no credentials, while the live containers are read only to copy their image or count their rows.

The drill restores the three dumps that matter most and judges each: forge-db into a scratch Postgres with its repository, user and action-run counts compared against the live forge; forge-data untarred into a scratch directory with git fsck --connectivity-only run over every restored repository, not only the main one; and mc-service-mongo through mongorestore --archive --gzip with the collections counted. A drill passes when the forge database restores with no errors, fsck reports bad=0, and Mongo has more than 0 collections. It cannot run in CI - it needs the real host, repository and restic password - so it is an operator acceptance step and the runbook's drill log (one row per drill: date, snapshot, each restore's seconds and counts, result) is the record of what has been proven, not a test.

The post-spec-084 forge-db + forge-data restore is PROVEN: the restore drill run on 2026-10-31 against snapshot 443ebb58 (the third night on the new format) restored forge-db in 14 s with 0 errors and 2 repositories / 1 user matching the live forge, untarred forge-data in 23 s with fsck ok=2 bad=0, and restored mc-service-mongo in 2 s with 2,315 documents in 2 collections — a pass, recorded as a row in the runbook's drill log. The old forgejo dump SQL restore, proven 2026-07-05, is now the historical record rather than the interim fallback, and because a change to what the backup carries invalidates the previous proof, the next such change needs a drill row of its own.

The forge repositories are copied while the forge is live (there is no forge stop at 03:30), so a push that lands mid-copy can leave a ref ahead of the objects it points at in the archive; git fsck reports that on restore as a FSCK FAILED line naming the repository. It is the same exposure the old forgejo dump had, and it is documented rather than engineered around. A drill against the next night's snapshot distinguishes it from real damage: an error that disappears on a later snapshot was a push caught mid-copy, one that persists is corruption.

The uncompressed forge data tar's de-duplication benefit is measured, not merely argued: after the format change the repository grew by 389.6 MiB and 412.1 MiB on 2026-10-30/31 (576.2 MiB on 2026-11-01) against a 2 GiB target, down from 19.8-21.1 GiB per night, and the forge's share of a snapshot fell from 22.5 GB to about 0.80 GB. What remains is mostly forge-db, because pg_dump -Fc compresses itself and so barely de-duplicates between nights.

The shared fake-host harness has a second guard covering its own footprint: each makeShimEnv call writes roughly 20 MB of fixtures under TMPDIR and nothing removed them, so 2,418 leaked roots (50 GB) filled the sandbox disk on 2026-11-01. makeShimEnv now requires the node:test context and removes its root in that context's after hook whether the test passes or fails, so a caller cannot forget the cleanup, and host-shims-cleanup.test.mjs runs the shim suites under a private TMPDIR and asserts they leave no host-shims-* root behind — including from a deliberately failing test.

The post-spec-084 format's steady state is measured in the repository itself: on 2026-11-01 the newest snapshot (ff20c0fe) was 1.533 GiB with 12 snapshots retained, and the per-dump sizes were forge-db 202,727,910 B plus forge-data 601,910,272 B (a forge share of about 0.80 GB, from 22.5 GB), komodo 85,162,249 B, release-apks 639,088,640 B, mc-service Mongo 813,102 B, Keycloak 381,023 B, BFF Mongo 3,289 B and agent-db 670 B.

The registry excluded from the snapshot does not grow without bound: since spec 084 US5, scripts/registry-retention.mjs — configured by infrastructure-as-code/forgejo/registry-retention.yaml and run weekly by .forgejo/workflows/registry-retention.yml on Sundays 06:00 UTC — decides per package which versions to keep, protecting every digest pinned in an infrastructure-as-code/docker/*/.env.deploy at the newest promotion and the five before it (read from git history, so the workflow checks out with fetch-depth: 0) and keeping every mcm-app-android version under keepAll. The schedule itself never deletes: --apply is passed only by a workflow_dispatch whose apply input is true, and the script refuses it while the config says mode: report, so two independent keys must agree before a version is removed — which is what keeps the registry exclusion safe for a rollback to an older digest.
